title: “HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES”—FOUR WORDS THAT COULD DESTROY THE MAN YOU PRETEND TO BE
paragraphs: “HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES”—FOUR WORDS THAT COULD DESTROY THE MAN YOU PRETEND TO BE

God never commanded a husband merely to provide a house, pay the bills, or demand respect. He commanded him to love his wife like Christ loved the Church. And when you discover what that actually means, you may never look at your marriage—or yourself—the same way again.
There is a woman somewhere tonight lying beside a man who would fight a stranger for disrespecting her…
But will not apologize for the way he spoke to her.
A man who would work twelve hours to make sure she has food on the table…
But cannot give her twelve uninterrupted minutes to explain why her heart is hurting.
A man who would never allow another man to put his hands on her…
But has learned to wound her with words, silence, contempt, and indifference.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part?
He genuinely believes he is a good husband.
Because he provides.
Because he stays.
Because he has never cheated.
Because he comes home every night.
And those things matter. Faithfulness matters. Provision matters. Commitment matters.
But somewhere between the wedding vows and the weight of everyday life, he has forgotten something terrifying.
A man can be physically present in his marriage while being emotionally absent from his wife.
He can sleep beside her every night and still leave her feeling painfully alone.
He can know her favorite meal, her birthday, and her clothing size…
And no longer know what makes her cry.
Then one Sunday morning, he opens his Bible and reads a verse he has probably heard a hundred times.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Ephesians 5:25, KJV
And suddenly, those familiar words begin to sound less like a wedding decoration…
And more like a summons to repentance.
Because Paul did not say, “Husbands, love your wives when they deserve it.”
He did not say, “Love them when they are agreeable, affectionate, beautiful, peaceful, or easy to understand.”
He said something infinitely more demanding.
Love your wives as Christ loved the Church.
And brother, before you say you already do…
You need to look at what happened to Jesus.
Because the standard for a Christian husband is not the strongest man in the room.
It is the Savior who laid down His life.
And that changes everything.
The apostle Paul wrote these words in Greek:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
Ephesians 5:25
A close English rendering is:
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Notice the word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate).
It comes from the Greek verb agapaō, meaning “to love.”
Here it is a present active imperative, second-person plural.
In plain language, Paul is commanding husbands to love.
This is not merely a suggestion to feel something romantic.
It is a command that calls for deliberate, ongoing action.
The grammatical form does not mean a husband must experience the same emotional intensity every moment. It means love is not optional simply because emotions fluctuate.
There will be mornings when your wife is exhausted.
There will be seasons when the children consume nearly every ounce of her attention.

There will be financial pressure, illness, disagreements, disappointment, aging, grief, and ordinary days when marriage feels less like a beautiful photograph and more like two tired people trying to survive another week.
And still, the command remains.
Love her.
Not because every day is easy.
But because Christ is your example.
Now look at another word in the same verse.
παρέδωκεν (paredōken).
It comes from paradidōmi, a verb that can mean “to hand over,” “deliver,” or “give up.”
Paul says Christ gave Himself up for the Church.
The verb points to the historical reality of Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
Jesus did not merely announce His love from a safe distance.
He demonstrated it.
He entered suffering.
He bore rejection.
He endured the cross.
And He willingly gave Himself for the people He came to redeem.
This does not mean a husband's suffering can atone for his wife's sins. Only Jesus Christ is the Savior.
It means a husband's love must be shaped by the self-giving character of the Savior's love.
And here is where the verse becomes deeply uncomfortable.
If your understanding of marriage always places your comfort first, you have not yet understood the love Paul is describing.
You may have understood authority.
You may have understood responsibility.
You may have understood the cultural expectations of being a husband.
But have you understood the cross?
Because the cross confronts the selfishness that quietly destroys marriages.
It confronts the husband who believes an apology makes him weak.
The husband who uses financial provision to excuse emotional neglect.
The husband who quotes Scripture when he wants obedience but ignores Scripture when it demands tenderness.
The husband who expects his wife to understand his stress but dismisses hers as complaining.
The husband who wants admiration without accountability.
And the husband who knows how to lead a meeting, manage a business, or command respect in public…
But does not know how to speak gently to the woman he promised to cherish.
This is not written to humiliate men.
It is written because the Gospel is too precious to be reduced to religious language that never transforms our homes.
And because some husbands desperately need to hear a truth that nobody has loved them enough to say.
You cannot use the Bible to demand honor while refusing to let the Bible confront your own heart.
Read Ephesians 5 carefully.
Before Paul addresses husbands and wives, he writes about being filled with the Spirit and about believers submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.
Ephesians 5:18–21 establishes a larger context of Spirit-shaped Christian living.
Then Paul addresses marriage.
Yes, the passage speaks about the husband as head of the wife.
Yes, Christians have differed over precisely how marital headship and submission should be understood and practiced.
But one thing cannot be honestly removed from Paul's instruction.
Whatever a husband believes about his role, he is commanded to love his wife in the pattern of Christ's sacrificial care.
And Jesus did not use His authority as an excuse for selfishness.
He said:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
Mark 10:45, KJV
Do you see the difference?
The world often teaches men to ask, “How much respect am I receiving?”
Christ teaches His followers to consider how faithfully they are serving.
The world admires the man who can control everyone around him.
Jesus reveals greatness through humble service.
The world celebrates the man who always wins the argument.
But a Christian husband must sometimes ask whether winning the argument has become more important to him than loving his wife.
Imagine this.
Your wife has been quiet all evening.
You ask what is wrong.
She says, “Nothing.”
But you know something is wrong.
Finally, she tells you.
She feels invisible.
She feels like every conversation becomes a competition.
She feels that you listen only long enough to defend yourself.
And before she finishes speaking, you interrupt.
“I work hard for this family. What more do you want from me?”
Silence.
She looks down.
And something inside her closes.
You think the argument is over because she stopped talking.
But silence does not always mean peace.
Sometimes it means someone has become too exhausted to keep explaining their pain.
Now imagine a different response.
You sit beside her.
You put your phone down.
You listen without preparing your defense.
And you say something that pride has been resisting for years.
“I didn't realize how alone you've been feeling. I want to understand. I'm sorry for the ways I've hurt you.”
No dramatic music.
No audience.
No applause.
Just a husband allowing humility to enter a room where pride has lived for too long.
That is not weakness.
That is a small but meaningful expression of repentance.
And repentance is not simply saying, “I'm sorry.”
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a change of mind and direction that involves turning away from sin.
In the Christian life, genuine repentance bears fruit.
It changes behavior.
It does not demand immediate forgiveness as payment for an apology.
It does not say, “I apologized yesterday. Why are you still hurt?”
It does not use tears to escape accountability.
It takes responsibility.
It makes room for the consequences of wrongdoing.
And where trust has been damaged, it patiently participates in rebuilding what was broken.
Some marriages do not need another expensive anniversary dinner as much as they need a sincere confession.
Some wives do not need another public declaration of love as much as they need private evidence of change.
Some husbands do not need another sermon about their position in the household.
They need to kneel before Christ and ask Him to expose the pride they have mistaken for strength.
And perhaps that husband is reading these words right now.
Perhaps you have been faithful with your paycheck but careless with your tongue.
Perhaps you have never committed adultery, yet you have allowed your heart to grow cold.
Perhaps you have been so determined to be respected that you have forgotten how to be gentle.
Perhaps your wife has been asking for the same change for years.
And perhaps, deep down, you know she has not been asking for perfection.
She has been asking to be heard.
Brother, do not turn this moment into another opportunity to defend yourself.
Bring it before God.
Because the Holy Spirit does not expose sin merely to leave us drowning in shame.
He convicts us and directs us toward Christ, in whom forgiveness and transformation are found.
And there is more.
Paul continues:
“So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.”
Ephesians 5:28, KJV
Think about that.
Paul connects a husband's treatment of his wife with the care he gives his own body.
When your body is hungry, you feed it.
When you are injured, you seek relief.
When you are exhausted, you recognize your need for rest.
Yet how easily can a man become attentive to his own discomfort while remaining indifferent to his wife's?
You notice immediately when your phone battery is low.
But have you noticed when her emotional strength is running low?
You recognize when the car needs maintenance.
But do you recognize when your marriage needs intentional attention?
You know when work is becoming overwhelming.
But do you know what has been overwhelming her?
This does not mean a husband must become a mind reader.
Marriage requires honest communication from both spouses.
But love does require attention.
It requires the willingness to learn.
It requires caring enough to ask and remaining present long enough to hear the answer.
And then Paul uses two beautiful verbs in Ephesians 5:29.
ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei) — “nourishes.”
θάλπει (thalpei) — “cherishes” or “cares for tenderly.”
These words describe the care a person gives his own body, which Paul connects to Christ's care for the Church.
Nourishing is not merely keeping someone alive.
It is contributing to their well-being.
Cherishing is not merely tolerating someone's presence.
It is treating that person as precious.

A husband who loves biblically should therefore be concerned not only with whether his wife has food, shelter, and clothing, but also with whether his conduct reflects patience, kindness, faithfulness, and care.
Does she feel safe telling you the truth?
Can she disagree without being threatened?
Can she express hurt without being mocked?
Does she know that her dignity matters even when you are angry?
Can she trust that your private behavior will reflect the faith you profess in public?
These are not small questions.
They reach into the heart of Christian discipleship.
And Scripture becomes even more direct.
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.”
Colossians 3:19, KJV
The Greek says:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς.
The verb pikrainesthe is related to bitterness and harshness.
Paul does not merely command husbands to love.
He also warns them against becoming embittered toward their wives.
That matters because bitterness rarely announces itself as bitterness.
Sometimes it sounds like sarcasm.
Sometimes it looks like contempt.
Sometimes it hides behind cold silence.
Sometimes it becomes a pattern of cutting remarks disguised as jokes.
Sometimes it turns every disagreement into a record of old offenses.
And sometimes a man becomes so accustomed to his harshness that he no longer recognizes it.
But Christ calls His people to something different.
Consider 1 Peter 3:7.
Peter instructs husbands to live with their wives according to knowledge and to show them honor as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
That phrase is extraordinary.
Fellow heirs of the grace of life.
Your wife is not a lesser soul.
She is not your servant.
She is not a possession you purchased with a wedding ring.
She is a person made in God's image.
And if she belongs to Christ, she is your fellow heir of His grace.
The same Savior who died for you is the Savior who died for her.
The same grace you desperately need is the grace she desperately needs.
The same Lord before whom you will stand is the Lord before whom she will stand.
How, then, can you treat lightly someone whom God commands you to honor?
And Peter adds a sobering warning about husbands' prayers being hindered.
That does not mean every unanswered prayer is punishment for marital failure.
But it does mean that how a husband treats his wife is spiritually significant.
A man cannot simply separate his worship from his conduct at home.
He cannot assume that public religious activity makes private cruelty irrelevant.
He cannot sing loudly about God's mercy while refusing to show mercy to those closest to him.
And he cannot excuse abuse by appealing to biblical authority.
Let this be unmistakably clear.
Sacrificial love is never permission for violence, coercion, intimidation, sexual abuse, or controlling behavior.
Christlike leadership cannot be used to justify sin against another person.
A wife is not commanded to remain in immediate danger to prove her faith.
Where abuse exists, safety, appropriate outside support, and genuine accountability matter. Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for protection or automatically restore trust.
And where a husband has harmed his wife, repentance requires more than religious promises. It requires ending the harmful behavior and accepting accountability.
Because the Jesus who calls us to love is also the Lord who loves righteousness.
Now perhaps another man is reading this, and his heart is breaking for a different reason.
He has tried.
He has worked.
He has prayed.
He has sought reconciliation.
He has admitted his failures.
And still, his marriage is painful.
He wonders whether being a godly husband means silently accepting every wrong done to him.
It does not.
Christlike love is not the abandonment of truth, wisdom, or appropriate boundaries.
A husband can be gentle without becoming passive.
He can forgive without pretending that sin has no consequences.
He can pursue peace without denying reality.
He can seek wise pastoral care, counseling, and other appropriate help when his marriage is struggling.
And he must remember that he cannot force another person's heart to change.
His calling is to be faithful to Christ in what belongs to his own responsibility.
The Gospel never promises that one person's obedience will automatically produce a perfect marriage.
But it does call every believer to walk in the light.
And that brings us to the part of this passage that may be the most beautiful of all.
Paul does not stop with husbands.
He points beyond marriage itself.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, he recalls the biblical truth that a man and woman become one flesh, then says that he is speaking of a profound mystery concerning Christ and the Church.
Marriage, in Paul's teaching, is connected to a reality greater than itself.
It points toward the covenant love of Christ for His people.
And that means a Christian husband's love is not ultimately about displaying how impressive he is.
It is about reflecting, however imperfectly, the character of Jesus.
A husband is not the savior of his wife.
He cannot cleanse her from sin.
He cannot replace the Holy Spirit.
He cannot carry the divine responsibilities that belong to Christ alone.
But he can reflect something of Christ's love through faithfulness, tenderness, truthfulness, humility, and sacrificial care.
And perhaps this is why the command is so demanding.
Because it does not merely ask, “Do you love your wife?”
It asks something deeper.
Does the way you love your wife increasingly resemble the love you have received from Jesus?
That question reaches beyond flowers.
Beyond anniversaries.
Beyond romantic photographs.
Beyond the public image of a happy Christian family.
It reaches the moment when you are tired and she needs you to listen.
The moment when you are angry and must choose your words.
The moment when you have sinned and must confess without excuses.
The moment when she is weak and needs compassion.
The moment when you disagree and must remember that she is not your enemy.
The moment when no one is watching.
Especially then.
Because Christian character is not measured only by what people see on Sunday.
It is also revealed in how we behave on an ordinary Tuesday evening when we are frustrated, disappointed, and nobody is applauding.
Stay here for a moment.
Not because you should drown in guilt.
But because there is hope for the man who is willing to repent.
Maybe your father never taught you how to love gently.
Maybe you grew up in a home where affection was rare and anger was normal.
Maybe the men around you taught you that admitting wrong was weakness.
Maybe you learned to survive by hiding your emotions.
Those experiences can help explain your struggles.
But they do not excuse hurting someone else.
And they do not have to determine the rest of your story.
Through Jesus Christ, you are not condemned to repeat every destructive pattern you inherited.
The Gospel announces forgiveness for sinners who turn to Christ in faith.
It also calls believers into a new way of living.
Paul writes:
2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
This is not a promise that every sinful habit disappears overnight.
It is the announcement of a new reality in Christ.
The Christian life involves ongoing repentance, renewal, and growth.
And that includes the way a man loves his wife.
Maybe you cannot undo the harsh words you spoke five years ago.
Maybe you cannot recover every evening you spent staring at a screen while she sat beside you feeling forgotten.
Maybe you cannot erase the moments when pride mattered more than tenderness.
But you can confess your sin today.
You can stop making excuses.
You can seek help where you need it.
You can begin practicing faithfulness in ways that are visible, specific, and sustained.
You can become a man who listens.
A man who keeps his word.
A man who prays with humility.
A man who does not confuse authority with entitlement.
A man whose wife does not have to fear his temper.
A man who understands that strength under the lordship of Christ includes self-control.
And when you fail again, as imperfect people sometimes do, you can return to the Lord in repentance rather than hiding behind religious appearances.
Not because your obedience earns salvation.
But because grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 reminds us that the grace of God instructs believers to live differently.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us through Christ and trains us to walk in godliness.
And there is something profoundly moving about a man who finally understands this.
He stops asking only, “Why doesn't she respect me?”
And begins asking, “Lord, where have I failed to love?”
He stops rehearsing every wrong his wife has committed.
And begins confessing the wrongs he has committed.
He stops using his upbringing as a permanent excuse.
And begins allowing Christ to reshape the man he is becoming.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
But sincerely.
Day by day.
And perhaps, one evening, he sits across from his wife and says:

“I've been reading Ephesians 5, and I realize I've been expecting things from you while neglecting what God has commanded of me. I have hurt you in ways I kept minimizing. I don't want to keep living like that. I'm sorry. I know words aren't enough, and I don't expect you to trust me immediately. But I want to change, and I'm willing to get help and be accountable.”
Maybe she cries.
Maybe she remains quiet.
Maybe she is not ready to believe him.
And if trust has been broken repeatedly, that response may be understandable.
He does not demand that the moment become a beautiful ending.
He understands that genuine change must be demonstrated over time.
Because repentance is not a performance designed to obtain forgiveness on demand.
It is a turning toward God that bears fruit in the way we live.
And sometimes the first evidence of a changed heart is simply this:
A man who once refused correction has finally become willing to listen.
Brother, this is where I want to speak directly to you.
Your wife does not need you to become Jesus.
You cannot.
She needs you to belong to Jesus and take His commands seriously.
She needs your love to be more than a statement.
More than a wedding vow you remember on anniversaries.
More than a Facebook post about how blessed you are.
She needs the daily reality of a man who is learning to love as Christ has called him to love.
And if you are unmarried, do not wait until your wedding day to begin developing that character.
Learn humility now.
Learn self-control now.
Learn to honor women as people made in God's image now.
Learn to confess your sins now.
A wedding ceremony does not automatically transform selfishness into sacrificial love.
Only the transforming work of God's grace can produce the kind of character marriage requires.
And to the wives reading this who have quietly carried years of disappointment, hear this too.
Your worth is not determined by your husband's ability or failure to recognize it.
You are not invisible to God.
You do not have to pretend that harmful behavior is acceptable in order to be considered faithful.
And the Lord's command to husbands to love their wives is not evidence that women must carry the entire responsibility for keeping a marriage together.
Both spouses are accountable before God.
Both need grace.
Both are called to truth and holiness.
And neither is authorized to use Scripture as a weapon against the other.
Now consider the Gospel at the center of all of this.
Jesus Christ loved His Church and gave Himself for her.
He died for sinners.
He rose again.
He offers forgiveness and new life to those who repent and believe in Him.
The cross reveals the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection reveals the victory of our Savior.
And the grace of God makes transformation possible.
That is why the Christian message is not simply, “Men, try harder.”
It is, “Come to Christ.”
Because you cannot manufacture the fruit of the Spirit merely through willpower.
Galatians 5:22–23 speaks of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Imagine how many marriages would be changed if those qualities increasingly shaped the way husbands and wives treated each other.
Not through pretending.
Not through spiritual slogans.
But through hearts being renewed by the Holy Spirit and lives being brought into obedience to God's Word.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer whether you have been a good husband by the standards of the world.
Perhaps the question is whether you are willing to let Jesus confront and transform the parts of your heart that you have been protecting from Him.
Because the man who refuses to admit he is wrong cannot meaningfully repent of what he refuses to acknowledge.
And the man who keeps defending his pride may lose precious opportunities to show love.
So before you close this article, ask yourself something.
If your wife were asked privately whether she feels cherished by you, what would she say?
If she were asked whether your faith makes you more patient, more truthful, more gentle, and more accountable, what would she say?
If your children grow up and imitate the way you treat their mother, would you be grateful for the example they learned?
And if the Lord brought your hidden attitudes into the light today, would you be willing to surrender them?
Do not answer for the audience.
Answer before God.
Because the goal is not to look like a Christian husband.
The goal is to follow Christ.
And if you recognize sin in your life, there is a place to begin.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I have not always loved the way You have commanded me to love. Forgive my selfishness, pride, harshness, and indifference. Expose the sins I keep excusing. Teach me to honor my wife, listen with patience, speak with gentleness, and serve without resentment. Give me the courage to repent sincerely and the humility to accept accountability. Where I have caused harm, help me stop, take responsibility, and pursue what is right. Transform my heart through Your Word and Spirit. Let my marriage, my character, and my daily choices increasingly reflect Your grace. I cannot save myself, and I cannot change myself apart from You. My hope is in Your death and resurrection. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if that prayer expresses the honest desire of your heart, do not let this moment end with emotion alone.
Take one concrete step toward obedience.
Have the conversation you have been avoiding.
Offer the apology you have been resisting.
Seek the help you have been too proud to ask for.
Open the Bible together if it is safe and welcome.
Begin again with truth.
And keep walking in it.
If this message has convicted you, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
And if God has already been restoring your marriage, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your story may encourage someone who has almost given up hope.
There is a young man preparing for marriage who has never been taught what biblical love actually demands.
There is a wife who has been praying for her husband to understand the difference between providing for a family and cherishing the people in it.
And there is someone who needs to discover that the Gospel offers more than religious appearances.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to accuse your spouse.
But to make the truth of Scripture available to people who may never hear it otherwise.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, new Christians, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along. Everyone needs to hear the truth about the Savior who forgives sinners and changes lives.
And there is something else I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior exists because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed faithfully, consistently, and as widely as possible.
Behind every article, every devotional, every biblical reflection, and every resource is a desire to help people encounter God's Word and grow as disciples of Christ.
We want to keep that biblical nourishment available.
We want to reach marriages that are struggling, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, and people who have never truly understood the Gospel.
But continuing and expanding this work requires faithful support.
Think of it as a recurring ministry offering made freely and cheerfully, not under pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
But the deeper invitation is not about merchandise.
It is about discipleship.
About staying close to Scripture.
About allowing God's Word to challenge, comfort, correct, and nourish you.
About being part of a community that refuses to settle for shallow Christianity when Jesus calls us to follow Him with our whole lives.
You are no less welcome here.
Your encouragement matters.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share matters.
Because our mission has never been to build a following around ourselves.
It is to point people to the Savior.
The Savior who calls husbands to love.
The Savior who calls sinners to repent.
The Savior who restores what sin has broken according to His wisdom and grace.
The Savior who can take a proud man and teach him humility.
The Savior who can take a wounded heart and meet it with compassion.
The Savior who can transform a marriage, even when the journey requires time, accountability, difficult conversations, and patient obedience.
And now, brother, we return to where we began.
A woman lying beside her husband.
A man convinced that because he provides, he has already done enough.
A marriage that looks fine from the outside but carries unspoken pain behind closed doors.
And a Bible verse that refuses to leave the man alone.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Ephesians 5:25.
The command has not changed.
The standard has not changed.
And the grace of God is still sufficient to call sinners out of darkness and into a transformed life.
So love her when the house is quiet.
Love her when life is difficult.
Love her when nobody is watching.
Love her with truth, gentleness, faithfulness, humility, and action.
And when you discover how far short you have fallen, do not hide behind pride.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
And walk in obedience.
Because one day, the greatest testimony of your marriage may not be that you never struggled.
It may be that, by God's grace, you stopped allowing your pride to have the final word.
She may forget the gifts you bought her, but she may never forget the day your repentance finally became a love she could recognize.
